</svg>
      <span class="eyebrow eyebrow-amber" style="margin-top:.45rem">Topic 2 of 5</span>
      <h1 class="h-topic" style="margin:.4rem 0 .35rem">Fluids</h1>
      <p class="lede small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:0 0 .4rem">Fluids are liquids and gases. This topic explains why pressure grows with depth, why things float or sink, and how moving fluid can lift an aeroplane.</p>
      <p class="lede" data-detail="tech">
        A fluid — liquid or gas — cannot resist being reshaped, so it pushes <strong>equally in
        every direction</strong> and its pressure grows with depth. From those two facts fall
        everything else: why ships float, how hydraulic presses lift cars, and how a wing makes
        lift out of moving air.
      </p>

      <div class="card mt-4">
        <h2 class="h-sub" style="margin-top:0">Learning objectives</h2>
        <ul class="objectives">
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Define density and pressure, and compute pressure at depth with P = P₀ + ρgh.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>State Archimedes’ principle and predict floating depth from the density ratio.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Explain sinking, floating and apparent weight in terms of forces.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Apply the continuity equation A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ to a narrowing pipe.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Use Bernoulli’s equation qualitatively: faster flow, lower pressure — on wings and in venturis.</span></li>
        </ul>
      </div>
    </div>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="density">2.1 · Density and pressure</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Density is how tightly mass is packed; pressure is how hard a fluid pushes. Go deeper and the push grows, because more fluid weighs on you.</p>
      <dl class="defs">
        <div><dt>Density ρ — mass per unit volume</dt><dd>ρ = m/V, in <strong>kg/m³</strong>. Water: 1000 kg/m³ (a litre weighs a kilogram); air at sea level: about 1.2 kg/m³; steel: 7800 kg/m³.</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Pressure P — force per unit area</dt><dd>P = F/A, in <strong>pascals</strong> (Pa = N/m²). One atmosphere ≈ 101 kPa — the column of air above you presses with the weight of about a tonne on every square metre, and you do not feel it because your body pushes back equally.</dd></div>
      </dl>

      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="P = P_0 + \rho g h">P = P₀ + ρ·g·h</span>
        <span class="where">P₀ = pressure at the surface (usually 1 atm) · h = depth below it · ρ = fluid density</span>
      </div>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Pressure in a still fluid grows <strong>linearly with depth</strong>: every layer of fluid
        must support the weight of everything above it. Direction does not matter — pressure at a
        point pushes equally in all directions (Pascal), which is why a small force on a small
        piston becomes a big force on a big piston: <strong>F₂ = F₁·A₂/A₁</strong>, the hydraulic
        press.
      </p>

      <div class="callout callout-key">
        <div class="callout-title">Worked example</div>
        <p>What is the absolute pressure 10 m below a lake surface? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², P₀ = 101 kPa)</p>
        <p class="mono small">P = 101 000 + 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 101 000 + 98 100 = <b>199 kPa</b> ≈ 2 atm — every 10 m of water adds roughly one atmosphere.</p>
      </div>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="archimedes">2.2 · Archimedes’ principle</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Anything in a fluid gets pushed up by the weight of the fluid it shoves aside. That is why less-dense things float and denser things sink.</p>
      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="F_B = \rho_{\mathrm{fluid}}\, V_{\mathrm{displaced}}\, g">F<sub>B</sub> = ρ<sub>fluid</sub> · V<sub>displaced</sub> · g</span>
        <span class="where">the buoyant force equals the WEIGHT of the fluid pushed aside</span>
      </div>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Why does this force exist? Pressure grows with depth, so the fluid pushes up on the
        bottom face of a submerged body <strong>harder</strong> than it pushes down on the top
        face. The difference is exactly the weight of the displaced fluid — that is Archimedes’
        principle, and it yields the floating rule:
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Floats</strong> (ρ<sub>obj</sub> &lt; ρ<sub>fluid</sub>): the body settles until displaced weight = its own weight. Submerged fraction = ρ<sub>obj</sub>/ρ<sub>fluid</sub> — ice shows 8% of itself above the surface because 917/1000 ≈ 0.92 is below.</li>
        <li><strong>Sinks</strong> (ρ<sub>obj</sub> &gt; ρ<sub>fluid</sub>): even fully submerged, F<sub>B</sub> &lt; W. The floor supplies the rest as a normal force — the “apparent weight” underwater is W − F<sub>B</sub>.</li>
      </ul>

      <details class="dig dig-real" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Real world — steel ships and load lines</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p>
          A cargo ship is steel, eight times denser than water — but it is a steel <em>shell
          around air</em>. What floats is the ship’s <strong>average</strong> density. Load the
          hold until the average density passes water’s and the deck goes under; that is why hulls
          carry <strong>Plimsoll load lines</strong>, one mark per water type: a ship floats
          deeper in warm fresh water (ρ ≈ 997) than in cold seawater (ρ ≈ 1025).
        </p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <details class="dig dig-trap" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Common misconceptions</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p>1. “Heavier things sink.” A 100-tonne ship floats; a 5-gram steel bolt sinks. What matters is <em>density</em> — mass per volume — not mass.</p>
        <p>2. “Buoyancy increases with depth.” For a fully submerged, incompressible body it is constant: F<sub>B</sub> depends on displaced <em>volume</em>, and that does not grow as the body descends.</p>
        <p>3. “Floating means no forces act.” Floating is <em>equilibrium</em>: weight down, buoyancy up, equal magnitudes. The net force is zero because two real forces balance, not because forces stopped existing.</p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-arch-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">2.3 · Simulation — the buoyancy tank</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Put a block in a tank and change how dense it is. Watch it float or sink, with the upward and downward pushes drawn to scale.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Set the block’s density and volume, choose the fluid, then drag the block under and let it
        go. The arrows are drawn to scale: weight (rose) down, buoyancy (cyan) up, and the floor’s
        normal force (amber) once a sunk block comes to rest. The readouts recompute
        F<sub>B</sub> = ρ<sub>f</sub>·V<sub>sub</sub>·g every frame — watch them balance exactly
        when the block floats.
      </p>
    </section>

    <section class="section-tight wrap wrap-sim">
      <div class="panel reveal">
        <div class="panel-head">
          <h3 class="panel-title"><span class="dot" style="background:#b5d777"></span> Archimedes bench</h3>
          <p class="panel-sub">F<sub>B</sub> = ρ<sub>f</sub>·V<sub>sub</sub>·g · floats when ρ<sub>obj</sub> &lt; ρ<sub>f</sub></p>
          <div class="panel-actions">
            <div class="seg" id="arch-fluid" role="group" aria-label="Fluid">
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="1000" aria-pressed="true">Water</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="1025" aria-pressed="false">Seawater</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="900" aria-pressed="false">Oil</button>
            </div>
            <div class="seg" id="arch-shape" role="group" aria-label="Object shape">
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="cube" aria-pressed="true">Cube</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="ball" aria-pressed="false">Ball</button>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sim-grid">
          <div>
            <canvas id="sim-archimedes" class="sim-canvas" role="img"
                    aria-label="A tank of fluid with a draggable block that floats or sinks according to its density"></canvas>
            <div class="legend">
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f8aebe"></i> weight W = ρ<sub>obj</sub>Vg</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a8d3e0"></i> buoyancy F<sub>B</sub></span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f6d36b"></i> normal force N (on the floor)</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <div class="panel-body">
            <div class="ctl-stack">
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">ρ<sub>obj</sub></span> object density</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="arch-rhov">600 kg/m³</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="arch-rho" min="300" max="3000" step="10" value="600" aria-label="Object density in kilograms per cubic metre">
                <span class="ctl-hint">wood ≈ 600 · ice ≈ 917 · water = 1000 · steel ≈ 7800</span>
              </div>
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">V</span> object volume</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="arch-volv">2.0 L</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="arch-vol" min="0.5" max="5" step="0.1" value="2" aria-label="Object volume in litres">
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="readouts mt-4">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Weight W</span><span class="stat-value hl-amber" id="arch-weight">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Buoyancy F<sub>B</sub></span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="arch-buoy">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Net force</span><span class="stat-value" id="arch-net">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <div class="readouts mt-3">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Submerged</span><span class="stat-value hl-emerald" id="arch-subfr">—</span><span class="stat-sub">displaces <span id="arch-vsub">—</span></span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Verdict</span><span class="stat-value" id="arch-state">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3" id="arch-explain" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="bernoulli">2.4 · Moving fluids: continuity and Bernoulli</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">When a fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. That single idea explains wing lift, narrow-pipe suction and many everyday surprises.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Set a fluid in motion and two new rules appear. First, <strong>continuity</strong>: fluid
        is not created or destroyed, so whatever flows into a pipe must flow out — in a narrower
        section it must move <em>faster</em>:
      </p>
      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2">A₁·v₁ = A₂·v₂</span>
        <span class="where">narrower pipe ⇒ faster flow — the same litres per second, squeezed through less area</span>
      </div>
      <p>
        Second, <strong>Bernoulli</strong>: for steady, incompressible, frictionless flow along a
        streamline, the sum of pressure, kinetic and gravitational energy density is constant:
      </p>
      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}">P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant</span>
        <span class="where">the headline: where the fluid speeds up, its pressure DROPS</span>
      </div>
      <p>
        That counter-intuitive sentence — <strong>faster flow, lower pressure</strong> — powers
        most of the fluid world: a wing’s curved top surface runs air faster than the bottom, so
        the pressure above is lower and the pressure difference lifts the aeroplane; a venturi’s
        throat sucks fuel into a carburettor; wind over your roof lowers the pressure above it,
        which is why hurricanes lift roofs <em>off</em> rather than push them down.
      </p>

      <details class="dig dig-trap" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>The “equal transit time” myth</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p>
          Textbooks once claimed air splits at the leading edge and the two halves
          <em>meet again</em> at the trailing edge, forcing the longer top path to be faster.
          <strong>They do not meet.</strong> In real flow the air over the top arrives well
          <em>ahead</em> of the air underneath — it is faster still than the myth suggests.
          Lift comes from the wing deflecting air downward (Newton III) and from the pressure
          difference that goes with it (Bernoulli) — the two explanations are the same physics
          viewed two ways, and neither needs equal transit times.
        </p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-bern-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">2.5 · Simulation — Bernoulli visualiser</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Two scenes: air flowing over a wing (raise the angle and watch lift grow, then stall), and water speeding up through a narrow pipe while its pressure drops.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Two scenes. In <strong>aerofoil</strong> mode, particles stream past a wing: raise the
        angle of attack and watch the top-side flow speed up, the pressure difference grow, the
        lift arrow lengthen — until past 15° the flow separates and the wing <em>stalls</em>.
        In <strong>venturi</strong> mode, water accelerates through a throat; the manometer
        columns show the pressure drop that continuity + Bernoulli predict, computed live.
      </p>
    </section>

    <section class="section-tight wrap wrap-sim">
      <div class="panel reveal">
        <div class="panel-head">
          <h3 class="panel-title"><span class="dot" style="background:#b5d777"></span> Bernoulli visualiser</h3>
          <p class="panel-sub">P + ½ρv² = constant · A₁v₁ = A₂v₂</p>
          <div class="panel-actions">
            <div class="seg" id="bern-mode" role="group" aria-label="Scene">
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="wing" aria-pressed="true">Aerofoil</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="pipe" aria-pressed="false">Venturi pipe</button>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sim-grid">
          <div>
            <canvas id="sim-bernoulli" class="sim-canvas" role="img"
                    aria-label="Particles flowing past an aerofoil or through a venturi pipe, showing speed and pressure changes"></canvas>
            <div class="legend">
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a8d3e0"></i> flow particles</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#b5d777"></i> lift / faster stream</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f6d36b"></i> throat flow</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <div class="panel-body">
            <div class="ctl-stack">
              <div class="ctl" id="bern-ctl-v">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">v</span> wind speed</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="bern-vv">15 m/s</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="bern-v" min="2" max="40" step="1" value="15" aria-label="Wind speed in metres per second">
              </div>
              <div class="ctl" id="bern-ctl-aoa">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">α</span> angle of attack</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="bern-aoav">6°</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="bern-aoa" min="0" max="20" step="1" value="6" aria-label="Angle of attack in degrees">
                <span class="ctl-hint">stall begins around 15° — push past it</span>
              </div>
              <div class="ctl" id="bern-ctl-flow" style="display:none">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">v₁</span> flow in the wide section</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="bern-flowv">0.50 m/s</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="bern-flow" min="0.1" max="2" step="0.05" value="0.5" aria-label="Flow speed in the wide section, metres per second">
              </div>
              <div class="ctl" id="bern-ctl-ratio" style="display:none">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">d₂/d₁</span> throat ratio</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="bern-ratiov">d₂ = 5.0 cm</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="bern-ratio" min="0.2" max="0.9" step="0.05" value="0.5" aria-label="Throat diameter as a fraction of the wide section">
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="readouts mt-4">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="bern-l1">free-stream v</span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="bern-v1">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="bern-l2">v over the top</span><span class="stat-value hl-emerald" id="bern-v2">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="bern-l3">ΔP</span><span class="stat-value hl-amber" id="bern-dp">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="bern-l4">lift</span><span class="stat-value" id="bern-extra">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3"><span class="tag tag-emerald" id="bern-state">attached flow</span></p>
            <p class="sim-note mt-2 mono" data-detail="tech" id="bern-sub" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="check">2.6 · Check your understanding</h2>

      <details class="check">
        <summary>A 1200 kg car rests on a hydraulic lift. The car piston has 100× the area of the input piston. What force must you apply?</summary>
        <div class="answer">Pressure is transmitted unchanged (Pascal), so F scales with area: <b>F = 1200·g/100 ≈ 118 N</b> — about the push of a 12 kg weight. You pay for it in distance: your piston travels 100× farther.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>An object floats in water with 30% of its volume above the surface. What is its density?</summary>
        <div class="answer">70% submerged ⇒ ρ<sub>obj</sub> = 0.70 × 1000 = <b>700 kg/m³</b> — roughly oak or a very full rubbish bin.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>A 2 kg block (density 2500 kg/m³) hangs from a string, fully submerged in water. What does the string feel?</summary>
        <div class="answer">V = m/ρ = 2/2500 = 0.0008 m³ → F<sub>B</sub> = 1000 × 0.0008 × 9.81 = 7.85 N. Tension = W − F<sub>B</sub> = 19.6 − 7.85 = <b>11.8 N</b> — it feels about 40% lighter underwater.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Water flows at 1 m/s through a pipe whose diameter halves at a junction. How fast is it in the narrow section?</summary>
        <div class="answer">Area scales with diameter², so A₂ = A₁/4 and v₂ = 4·v₁ = <b>4 m/s</b>. Halving the <em>diameter</em> quadruples the speed — continuity bites hard.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Why do two ships sailing close side-by-side risk being pulled together?</summary>
        <div class="answer">Water squeezed between the hulls speeds up, and by Bernoulli its pressure drops below the pressure on the outer sides — the higher outside pressure pushes the ships together. The same effect slams a shower curtain inward while the water runs.</div>
      </details>

        <div class="flex flex-wrap items-center justify-between gap-3">

      <span class="eyebrow eyebrow-amber" style="margin-top:.45rem">Topic 3 of 5</span>
      <h1 class="h-topic" style="margin:.4rem 0 .35rem">Temperature &amp; heat</h1>
      <p class="lede small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:0 0 .4rem">Temperature says how hot something is; heat is energy moving from hot to cold. This topic covers the three scales, the energy maths of heating, and the three ways heat travels.</p>
      <p class="lede" data-detail="tech">
        <strong>Temperature</strong> says how fast the particles of a body are jittering on
        average; <strong>heat</strong> is energy on the move from hot to cold. Keeping those two
        apart — and knowing how energy travels — explains everything from sea breezes to
        thermos flasks.
      </p>

      <div class="card mt-4">
        <h2 class="h-sub" style="margin-top:0">Learning objectives</h2>
        <ul class="objectives">
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Convert confidently between °C, °F and K.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Distinguish temperature, heat and internal energy.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Solve specific-heat problems with Q = mcΔT, including phase changes.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Identify conduction, convection and radiation in real situations.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Explain why metals feel cold, why radiators sit under windows, and how a vacuum flask works.</span></li>
        </ul>
      </div>
    </div>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="scales">3.1 · Temperature and the three scales</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin are just three number labels for the same hotness. The converter below keeps them in step.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        A thermometer works by <strong>thermal equilibrium</strong>: put it in contact with
        something and wait, and the reading stops moving when both share the same temperature
        (the zeroth law of thermodynamics). Three scales describe that number:
      </p>

      <div class="table-scroll">
        <table class="data">
          <caption class="tiny faint" style="caption-side:top;text-align:left;padding:.4rem .2rem">Fixed points on the three scales</caption>
          <thead><tr><th>Landmark</th><th>°C</th><th>°F</th><th>K</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td class="txt">absolute zero</td><td>−273.15</td><td>−459.67</td><td>0</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">scales agree</td><td>−40</td><td>−40</td><td>233.15</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">water freezes</td><td>0</td><td>32</td><td>273.15</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">human body</td><td>37</td><td>98.6</td><td>310.15</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">water boils (1 atm)</td><td>100</td><td>212</td><td>373.15</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="T_F = \tfrac{9}{5}T_C + 32, \qquad T_K = T_C + 273.15">°F = °C × 9/5 + 32 &nbsp;·&nbsp; K = °C + 273.15</span>
        <span class="where">and the reverse: °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9 · °C = K − 273.15</span>
      </div>
      <p>
        Two habits prevent every conversion error: <strong>subtract the 32 before rescaling</strong>
        (it is an offset between zero points), and remember that <strong>a kelvin and a Celsius
        degree are the same size</strong> — only their zeroes differ. That is why temperature
        <em>differences</em> never need converting: ΔT = 10 °C = 10 K (though = 18 °F).
        Physics equations always want kelvin, because only kelvin starts at true zero motion.
      </p>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-thermo-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">3.2 · Simulation — the thermometer</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Drag the thermometer or use the slider. All three scales update together, with the conversion maths shown step by step.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Drag the mercury column or move the slider: all three scales update together, with the
        conversion arithmetic printed live. The dashed markers show the landmarks — freezing,
        body temperature, boiling — and the special crossing point at −40°.
      </p>
    </section>

    <section class="section-tight wrap wrap-sim">
      <div class="panel reveal">
        <div class="panel-head">
          <h3 class="panel-title"><span class="dot" style="background:#f8aebe"></span> Thermometer</h3>
          <p class="panel-sub">°F = °C × 9/5 + 32 · K = °C + 273.15</p>
          <div class="panel-actions">
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-thermo-preset="-40">−40°</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-thermo-preset="0">Freezing</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-thermo-preset="37">Body</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-thermo-preset="100">Boiling</button>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sim-grid">
          <div>
            <canvas id="sim-thermometer" class="sim-canvas" role="img"
                    aria-label="A draggable thermometer showing the same temperature in Celsius, Fahrenheit and kelvin"></canvas>
            <div class="legend">
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f8aebe"></i> mercury column</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a8d3e0"></i> landmark markers</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <div class="panel-body">
            <div class="ctl-stack">
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">T</span> temperature</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="thermo-Tv">20.0 °C</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="thermo-T" min="-80" max="250" step="0.5" value="20" aria-label="Temperature in degrees Celsius">
                <span class="ctl-hint">or type an exact value:
                  <input class="inp" type="number" id="thermo-Tnum" min="-80" max="250" step="0.5" value="20" style="width:7rem;display:inline-block;margin-left:.35rem" aria-label="Exact temperature in degrees Celsius"> °C
                </span>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="readouts mt-4">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Celsius</span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="thermo-C">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Fahrenheit</span><span class="stat-value hl-amber" id="thermo-F">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Kelvin</span><span class="stat-value hl-emerald" id="thermo-K">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3 mono" data-detail="tech" id="thermo-sub" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
            <p class="sim-note mt-2" id="thermo-note">—</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="heat">3.3 · Heat and specific heat capacity</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Heating something takes energy: more mass or a bigger temperature rise costs more. Water soaks up a lot of energy, which is why it is used for cooling.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        <strong>Heat Q</strong> is energy transferred because of a temperature difference — it
        flows spontaneously from hot to cold and is measured in joules. How much a body’s
        temperature rises per joule depends on its mass and its material:
      </p>
      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="Q = mc\,\Delta T">Q = m·c·ΔT</span>
        <span class="where">m in kg · c = specific heat capacity in J/(kg·K) · ΔT in K (or °C — the step size is identical)</span>
      </div>

      <div class="table-scroll">
        <table class="data">
          <caption class="tiny faint" style="caption-side:top;text-align:left;padding:.4rem .2rem">Specific heat capacities you should recognise</caption>
          <thead><tr><th>Material</th><th>c, J/(kg·K)</th><th>What it means</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td class="txt">water (liquid)</td><td>4186</td><td class="txt">huge — oceans store summer heat for winter</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">ice</td><td>2100</td><td class="txt">half of liquid water</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">aluminium</td><td>900</td><td class="txt">heats fast — good for pans</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">iron / steel</td><td>450</td><td class="txt">a frying pan handle’s problem</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">copper</td><td>385</td><td class="txt">even faster to heat</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <p>
        During a <strong>phase change</strong> the temperature stands still: every joule goes into
        breaking bonds instead of speeding particles up. Water needs
        <strong>L<sub>f</sub> = 334 kJ/kg</strong> to melt and a remarkable
        <strong>L<sub>v</sub> = 2260 kJ/kg</strong> to boil — five times more energy to vaporise
        water at 100 °C than to heat it from 20 to 100 °C. That is why steam burns so badly:
        it dumps its latent heat into your skin <em>before</em> it even cools down.
      </p>

      <div class="callout callout-key">
        <div class="callout-title">Worked example — the kettle</div>
        <p>How much energy to boil 1 kg of water from 20 °C? And how long in a 2.2 kW kettle?</p>
        <p class="mono small">Q = mcΔT = 1 × 4186 × 80 = <b>335 kJ</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; t = Q/P = 335 000/2200 ≈ <b>152 s ≈ 2½ min</b> (real kettles take a little longer — losses).</p>
      </div>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="transfer">3.4 · The three ways heat moves</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Heat moves three ways: through contact (conduction), through circulating fluids (convection), and as invisible waves that cross empty space (radiation).</p>
      <dl class="defs">
        <div><dt>Conduction — contact, particle to particle</dt><dd>Vibrating atoms and (in metals) free electrons pass energy along a material without the material moving. Rate ∝ k·A·ΔT/L: k is the thermal conductivity — copper 401 W/(m·K), glass 1.0, wood 0.15, air 0.026. Still air is an <em>insulator</em>; that is what fleeces, double glazing and loft wool are really trapping.</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Convection — the fluid itself travels</dt><dd>Heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler fluid sinks to replace it, setting up a circulation loop. Convection needs a fluid and gravity: radiators sit under windows to intercept sinking cold air, and there is no convection aboard the ISS.</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Radiation — electromagnetic waves</dt><dd>Every body radiates; output grows as T⁴ (Stefan–Boltzmann, P = εσAT⁴), which is why a small temperature rise means much more radiation. It needs <strong>no medium at all</strong> — sunlight crosses 150 million km of vacuum. Matt black surfaces absorb and emit best (ε ≈ 0.95); shiny surfaces reflect (ε ≈ 0.05).</dd></div>
      </dl>

      <details class="dig dig-trap" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Common misconceptions</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p data-detail="tech">1. “Heat rises.” Heat is not a substance. <em>Hot air</em> rises because it is less dense — that is convection. In a vacuum, nothing rises; radiation still travels in straight lines.</p>
        <p>2. “Metal feels cold, so metal is colder.” On a table indoors, the metal and the wood are at exactly the same temperature — your skin is the thermometer, and metal conducts your heat away faster.</p>
        <p>3. “A coat warms you up.” A coat generates nothing; it slows the loss of <em>your</em> heat. Wrap one around an ice cube and the ice melts <em>more slowly</em>.</p>
        <p>4. “ΔT must be converted to kelvin before using Q = mcΔT.” No — a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so differences pass through untouched. Only <em>absolute</em> temperatures (as in gas laws or T⁴) need kelvin.</p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-heat-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">3.5 · Simulation — heat transfer lab</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Three scenes you can switch between: heat spreading along a rod, water circulating in a pot, and warmth radiating across a gap. The settings change what you see.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Three scenes, one canvas. <strong>Conduction:</strong> hold one end of a rod hot and watch
        the temperature profile relax to steady state — then swap copper for wood and see the flux
        collapse by a factor of thousands. <strong>Convection:</strong> a heater drives a visible
        circulation loop; more power, faster plume. <strong>Radiation:</strong> move the plates
        away from the source and watch intensity fall as 1/d² — and compare what matt black and
        shiny surfaces absorb.
      </p>
    </section>

              </div>

              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="readouts mt-4">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="ht-r1l">hot end</span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="ht-r1">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="ht-r2l">cold end</span><span class="stat-value" id="ht-r2">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="ht-r3l">heat flux</span><span class="stat-value hl-amber" id="ht-r3">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label" id="ht-r4l">k</span><span class="stat-value" id="ht-r4">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3 mono" data-detail="tech" id="ht-sub" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
            <p class="sim-note mt-2" id="ht-note">—</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="check">3.6 · Check your understanding</h2>

      <details class="check">
        <summary>Convert −196 °C (liquid nitrogen) to °F and K.</summary>
        <div class="answer">K = −196 + 273.15 = <b>77.15 K</b>. °F = −196 × 9/5 + 32 = −352.8 + 32 = <b>−320.8 °F</b>.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>How much heat raises 0.5 kg of aluminium from 20 °C to 180 °C? (c = 900 J/kg·K)</summary>
        <div class="answer">Q = mcΔT = 0.5 × 900 × 160 = <b>72 kJ</b>. The same change in water would need 0.5 × 4186 × 160 = 335 kJ — nearly five times more, which is why pans are metal and their contents are wet.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>A 0.5 kW heater radiates into a room. If you triple your distance from it, how much intensity reaches you?</summary>
        <div class="answer">Intensity follows the inverse square law: I = P/(4πd²). Tripling d divides I by <b>9</b> — you feel one ninth of the warmth.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Name the dominant heat-transfer mechanism: (a) a spoon handle warming in soup, (b) a fridge coil cooling air at the top of the compartment, (c) feeling a fire on your face from 3 m away.</summary>
        <div class="answer">(a) <b>Conduction</b> through the metal. (b) <b>Convection</b> — cooled air is denser and sinks, setting up the loop. (c) <b>Radiation</b> — the air between you and the fire is barely warmed; infrared crosses the gap (and would cross a vacuum).</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Why does a vacuum flask keep coffee hot for hours?</summary>
        <div class="answer">It attacks all three mechanisms at once: the <b>vacuum</b> between the walls kills conduction and convection (no particles to carry energy), the <b>silvered walls</b> reflect radiation back (low emissivity), and the <b>stopper</b> blocks convection and evaporation at the only remaining opening.</div>
      </details>

      <div class="card mt-4">
        <div class="flex flex-wrap items-center justify-between gap-3">
          <div>

      <span class="eyebrow eyebrow-amber" style="margin-top:.45rem">Topic 1 of 5</span>
      <h1 class="h-topic" style="margin:.4rem 0 .35rem">Measurement &amp; vectors</h1>
      <p class="lede small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:0 0 .4rem">Physics starts with measuring things. This topic teaches two tools you will use everywhere: checking units, and adding arrows (vectors) the correct way.</p>
      <p class="lede" data-detail="tech">
        Physics is a science of <strong>measured numbers</strong> — and every number carries a unit.
        Before any of the later topics make sense, you need two tools: <strong>dimensional
        analysis</strong>, which catches algebra mistakes before they happen, and
        <strong>vectors</strong>, which let a single arrow carry both a size and a direction.
      </p>

      <div class="card mt-4">
        <h2 class="h-sub" style="margin-top:0">Learning objectives</h2>
        <ul class="objectives">
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Name the SI base units and convert between prefixes (k, m, µ, n).</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Check any equation with dimensional analysis and derive units from definitions.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Distinguish scalars from vectors and resolve a vector into components.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Add vectors graphically (tip-to-tail, parallelogram) and by components.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Compute the magnitude and direction of a resultant, and place it in the right quadrant.</span></li>
        </ul>
      </div>
    </div>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="units">1.1 · Units and the SI system</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Every measurement is a number with a unit, like 5 kg. Using the same standard units everywhere is what stops costly mix-ups.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Every measurement in physics is a <strong>number times a unit</strong> — and the number is
        meaningless without it. The <em>Système International</em> (SI) defines seven
        <strong>base units</strong>; everything else is built from them.
      </p>

      <div class="table-scroll">
        <table class="data">
          <caption class="tiny faint" style="caption-side:top;text-align:left;padding:.4rem .2rem">The seven SI base units</caption>
          <thead><tr><th>Quantity</th><th>Unit</th><th>Symbol</th><th>Everyday anchor</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td class="txt">Length</td><td>metre</td><td>m</td><td class="txt">a little over half a door height</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Mass</td><td>kilogram</td><td>kg</td><td class="txt">a litre bottle of water</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Time</td><td>second</td><td>s</td><td class="txt">one heartbeat</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Electric current</td><td>ampere</td><td>A</td><td class="txt">a phone charger draws ~0.5–2 A</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Temperature</td><td>kelvin</td><td>K</td><td class="txt">room temperature ≈ 293 K</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Amount of substance</td><td>mole</td><td>mol</td><td class="txt">6.022×10<sup>23</sup> particles</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Luminous intensity</td><td>candela</td><td>cd</td><td class="txt">one candle, roughly</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <p>
        <strong>Derived units</strong> are products of base units with their own names: the newton
        (N = kg·m/s², force), the joule (J = N·m, energy), the watt (W = J/s, power), the pascal
        (Pa = N/m², pressure) — you will meet all four in the topics that follow.
        <strong>Prefixes</strong> scale a unit by powers of ten: kilo (k, 10³), centi (c, 10⁻²),
        milli (m, 10⁻³), micro (µ, 10⁻⁶), nano (n, 10⁻⁹). One rule saves endless confusion:
        <em>a prefix belongs to its unit</em> — 1 km/s is 1000 m/s, never “kilo (m/s)”.
      </p>

      <details class="dig dig-real" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Real world — the $327 million unit error</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p>
          In 1999 NASA lost the <strong>Mars Climate Orbiter</strong> because one engineering team
          reported thruster impulses in pound-force seconds while the navigation software expected
          newton-seconds. The spacecraft approached Mars along the wrong trajectory and burned up.
          Unit bookkeeping is not pedantry — it is a safety system.
        </p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="dimensions">1.2 · Dimensional analysis</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">A quick sanity check for any formula: both sides must use the same kind of units. If they don't, the formula is wrong — no calculation needed.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Every physical quantity has <strong>dimensions</strong> built from mass [M], length [L] and
        time [T]. Velocity is length per time, [L][T]<sup>−1</sup>; acceleration is
        [L][T]<sup>−2</sup>; force is [M][L][T]<sup>−2</sup>. Two rules do all the work:
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li>You may only <strong>add or compare quantities with the same dimensions</strong> — “3 m + 5 s” is not a thing.</li>
        <li>Both sides of a valid equation have the <strong>same dimensions</strong>, and arguments of sin, exp, log… are <strong>dimensionless</strong>.</li>
      </ul>

      <div class="callout callout-key">
        <div class="callout-title">Worked example — check an equation before you trust it</div>
        <p>Is <span data-tex="v^2 = u^2 + 2as">v² = u² + 2as</span> dimensionally consistent?</p>
        <p class="mono small">
          [v²] = [L]²[T]<sup>−2</sup> &nbsp;·&nbsp; [u²] = [L]²[T]<sup>−2</sup> ✓ &nbsp;·&nbsp;
          [2as] = [L][T]<sup>−2</sup> × [L] = [L]²[T]<sup>−2</sup> ✓ — all three terms match, so the
          equation <em>could</em> be right. (It is — that is the constant-acceleration formula.)
        </p>
        <p>Dimensional analysis cannot catch a wrong pure number (a missing ½), but it catches every wrong <em>shape</em> instantly.</p>
      </div>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="vectors">1.3 · Vectors and components</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Some quantities (like force or velocity) have a direction as well as a size, so we draw them as arrows. To add arrows, split each into horizontal and vertical parts, add the parts, then recombine.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        A <strong>scalar</strong> has magnitude only (mass, temperature, time, energy).
        A <strong>vector</strong> has magnitude <em>and</em> direction (displacement, velocity,
        force, acceleration) and obeys vector addition. Walking 3 km east then 4 km north does not
        put you 7 km away — it puts you <strong>5 km</strong> away, because displacements add as
        arrows, not as numbers.
      </p>

      <figure class="fig">
        <div class="fig-box">
          <svg viewBox="0 0 560 240" width="560" height="240" role="img"
               aria-label="A vector A resolved into horizontal component Ax and vertical component Ay, with the resultant of A plus B drawn as the parallelogram diagonal.">
            <g stroke="rgba(148,163,184,.25)" stroke-width="1">
              <path d="M60 200H520M60 150H520M60 100H520M60 50H520"/>
              <path d="M110 20V200M160 20V200M210 20V200M260 20V200M310 20V200M360 20V200M410 20V200M460 20V200"/>
            </g>
            <g stroke="#5b7299" stroke-width="2"><path d="M60 20V200H520"/></g>
            <!-- vector A with components -->
            <g stroke-width="3" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round">
              <path d="M60 200 L260 60" stroke="#a8d3e0"/>
              <path d="M260 60 L245 72 M260 60 L262 79" stroke="#a8d3e0"/>
              <path d="M60 200 H260" stroke="#7b8db0" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
              <path d="M260 200 V60" stroke="#7b8db0" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
            </g>
            <text x="160" y="218" fill="#a9bad6" font-size="13" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Ax = A·cos θ</text>
            <text x="292" y="135" fill="#a9bad6" font-size="13" font-family="monospace">Ay = A·sin θ</text>
            <text x="140" y="115" fill="#a8d3e0" font-size="14" font-family="monospace" font-weight="700">A</text>
            <path d="M95 200 A 45 45 0 0 0 97 174" stroke="#f6d36b" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
            <text x="112" y="188" fill="#f6d36b" font-size="13" font-family="monospace">θ</text>
            <!-- parallelogram addition -->
            <g stroke-width="3" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round">
              <path d="M330 200 L420 130" stroke="#a8d3e0"/>
              <path d="M330 200 L380 90" stroke="#f6d36b"/>
              <path d="M420 130 L470 20 M380 90 L470 20" stroke="#d5b8d8" stroke-dasharray="6 5" stroke-width="2"/>
              <path d="M330 200 L470 20" stroke="#b5d777"/>
              <path d="M470 20 L452 26 M470 20 L466 39" stroke="#b5d777"/>
            </g>
            <text x="385" y="180" fill="#a8d3e0" font-size="13" font-family="monospace" font-weight="700">A</text>
            <text x="338" y="135" fill="#f6d36b" font-size="13" font-family="monospace" font-weight="700">B</text>
            <text x="480" y="30" fill="#b5d777" font-size="13" font-family="monospace" font-weight="700">R = A + B</text>
            <text x="196" y="26" fill="#a9bad6" font-size="12.5" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="700">RESOLVE</text>
            <text x="382" y="226" fill="#a9bad6" font-size="12.5" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="700">ADD (parallelogram = tip-to-tail)</text>
          </svg>
        </div>
        <figcaption>Figure 1 — Left: a vector split into components. Right: two vectors added as the diagonal of the parallelogram they span.</figcaption>
      </figure>

      <h3 class="h-sub">Components: the whole game</h3>
      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="A_x = A\cos\theta, \quad A_y = A\sin\theta">A<sub>x</sub> = A·cos θ &nbsp;·&nbsp; A<sub>y</sub> = A·sin θ</span>
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}, \quad \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right)">|A| = √(A<sub>x</sub>² + A<sub>y</sub>²) &nbsp;·&nbsp; θ = tan⁻¹(A<sub>y</sub>/A<sub>x</sub>)</span>
        <span class="where">θ measured from the +x axis; signs of A<sub>x</sub>, A<sub>y</sub> fix the quadrant</span>
      </div>
      <p>
        Adding vectors then becomes ordinary arithmetic <em>per direction</em>:
        <strong>R<sub>x</sub> = A<sub>x</sub> + B<sub>x</sub></strong> and
        <strong>R<sub>y</sub> = A<sub>y</sub> + B<sub>y</sub></strong>. Subtraction is addition of
        the negative: −B is B flipped 180°. Graphically the same answer appears as the
        <strong>tip-to-tail</strong> walk (put B’s tail on A’s tip; R closes the trip) or the
        <strong>parallelogram</strong> diagonal — both are drawn live in the simulator below.
      </p>

      <div class="callout callout-key">
        <div class="callout-title">Worked example</div>
        <p>A hiker walks 3 km east, then 4 km north. How far is she from the start, and in what direction?</p>
        <p class="mono small">R<sub>x</sub> = 3, R<sub>y</sub> = 4 → |R| = √(9+16) = <b>5 km</b>, θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) = <b>53.1° north of east</b>.</p>
      </div>

      <details class="dig dig-trap" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Common misconceptions</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p>1. “|A + B| = |A| + |B|.” Only when the vectors point the same way. In general the resultant lies between ||A| − |B|| and |A| + |B| — the simulator’s “cancel to zero” preset shows the extreme.</p>
        <p>2. “tan⁻¹ gives the direction.” It gives an angle, but the calculator cannot know your quadrant: A = (−3, +4) and A = (3, −4) have the same tangent. Always finish with the signs — sketch the arrow.</p>
        <p>3. “A negative vector points down.” Negative applies to a <em>component</em>, relative to your chosen axes. Choose axes along the slope and “negative x” means downhill along that slope.</p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-vector-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">1.4 · Simulation — vector addition bench</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Drag the two arrowheads. The green arrow is their combined effect and updates while you drag. The dashed lines show the two ways to picture the same addition.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Drag the two arrowheads. The resultant <strong>R = A + B</strong> redraws itself from the
        components every frame, and the dashed guides show the parallelogram it completes.
        Switch to <em>tip-to-tail</em> to see the same addition as a walk: B starts where A ends,
        and R closes the triangle. Try the presets — including one where the vectors cancel exactly.
      </p>
    </section>

    <section class="section-tight wrap wrap-sim">
      <div class="panel reveal">
        <div class="panel-head">
          <h3 class="panel-title"><span class="dot" style="background:#a8d3e0"></span> Vector addition bench</h3>
          <p class="panel-sub">R = A + B · |R| = √(Rx² + Ry²)</p>
          <div class="panel-actions">
            <div class="seg" id="vec-mode" role="group" aria-label="Addition layout">
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="parallelogram" aria-pressed="true">Parallelogram</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="tip" aria-pressed="false">Tip-to-tail</button>
            </div>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-vec-preset="3,0,0,4">3-4-5</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-vec-preset="3,4,4,-2">A=(3,4)</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-vec-preset="2,2,-2,-2">Cancel to zero</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-ghost" type="button" id="vec-reset">Reset</button>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sim-grid">
          <div>
            <canvas id="sim-vector-add" class="sim-canvas" role="img"
                    aria-label="Two draggable vectors from a common origin with their resultant drawn as the parallelogram diagonal"></canvas>
            <div class="legend">
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a8d3e0"></i> vector A</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f6d36b"></i> vector B</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#b5d777"></i> resultant R = A + B</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#d5b8d8"></i> parallelogram guides</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <div class="panel-body">
            <div class="readouts">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">|A|</span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="vec-Amag">—</span><span class="stat-sub">θ<sub>A</sub> <span id="vec-Aang">—</span></span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">|B|</span><span class="stat-value" style="color:#f6d36b" id="vec-Bmag">—</span><span class="stat-sub">θ<sub>B</sub> <span id="vec-Bang">—</span></span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">|R|</span><span class="stat-value hl-emerald" id="vec-Rmag">—</span><span class="stat-sub">θ<sub>R</sub> <span id="vec-Rang">—</span></span></div>
            </div>
            <div class="readouts mt-3">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">R<sub>x</sub> = A<sub>x</sub> + B<sub>x</sub></span><span class="stat-value" id="vec-Rx">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">R<sub>y</sub> = A<sub>y</sub> + B<sub>y</sub></span><span class="stat-value" id="vec-Ry">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3 mono" data-detail="tech" id="vec-sub" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
            <div class="callout callout-key mt-3">
              <div class="callout-title">Try this</div>
              <p class="small" style="margin:0">Drag B until R points straight up. What must B<sub>x</sub> equal? (Answer: −A<sub>x</sub> — the x-components cancel while the y-components add.)</p>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="check">1.5 · Check your understanding</h2>

      <details class="check">
        <summary>Express the joule in SI base units.</summary>
        <div class="answer">J = N·m = (kg·m/s²)·m = <b>kg·m²/s²</b> = kg·m²·s<sup>−2</sup>. (The watt is one step further: W = J/s = kg·m²·s<sup>−3</sup>.)</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>A vector of magnitude 10 points 30° above the +x axis. Find its components.</summary>
        <div class="answer">A<sub>x</sub> = 10·cos 30° = <b>8.66</b>, A<sub>y</sub> = 10·sin 30° = <b>5.00</b>. Check: √(8.66² + 5²) = √100 = 10 ✓.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Two forces of 5 N and 12 N act on the same point at right angles. What is the resultant?</summary>
        <div class="answer">√(25 + 144) = <b>13 N</b>, at tan⁻¹(12/5) = <b>67.4°</b> from the 5 N force — the 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Is the equation T = 2π√(L/g) for a pendulum’s period dimensionally consistent?</summary>
        <div class="answer"><b>Yes.</b> [L/g] = [L]/([L][T]<sup>−2</sup>) = [T]², so √(L/g) has dimensions [T], and 2π is dimensionless. (It is also physically correct — that is the real pendulum formula.)</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>You walk 6 km north, then 6 km south-east (45° below +x). Are you back where you started?</summary>
        <div class="answer"><b>No.</b> The second leg has components (6·cos45°, −6·sin45°) = (4.24, −4.24) km. Total displacement = (4.24, 6 − 4.24) = (4.24, 1.76) km — about <b>4.6 km away, 22.5° north of east</b>. Only an exactly opposite vector cancels.</div>
      </details>

  <path d="M38 26 C34 8 46 5 49 16" fill="#f6f1e5" stroke="#3a3d45" stroke-width="3" stroke-linecap="round"/>

</svg>
      <span class="eyebrow eyebrow-amber" style="margin-top:.45rem">Topic 4 of 5</span>
      <h1 class="h-topic" style="margin:.4rem 0 .35rem">Waves &amp; sound</h1>
      <p class="lede small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:0 0 .4rem">Waves carry energy without carrying material. This topic covers the vocabulary, the master equation v = fλ, and sound as a wave you can actually hear.</p>
      <p class="lede" data-detail="tech">
        A wave is a <strong>disturbance that travels, carrying energy without carrying matter</strong>.
        Ripples, sound, seismic tremors and light are all the same idea wearing different costumes —
        and one equation, v = fλ, ties them together.
      </p>

      <div class="card mt-4">
        <h2 class="h-sub" style="margin-top:0">Learning objectives</h2>
        <ul class="objectives">
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Define amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, with their units.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Apply v = fλ and T = 1/f to any periodic wave.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves, with examples.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Relate pitch to frequency and loudness to amplitude for sound.</span></li>
          <li><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M20 6 9 17l-5-5"/></svg><span>Explain why wave speed belongs to the medium, not the source.</span></li>
        </ul>
      </div>
    </div>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="describe">4.1 · Describing a wave</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Four numbers describe any wave: how tall it is (amplitude), the length of one cycle (wavelength), how many cycles per second (frequency), and the seconds per cycle (period).</p>
      <dl class="defs">
        <div><dt>Amplitude A — the biggest displacement</dt><dd>How far the medium swings from rest, in metres (or the field’s strength, for light). Amplitude carries the <strong>energy</strong>: double A and a wave carries four times the energy.</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Wavelength λ — one complete cycle, in space</dt><dd>Crest to crest (or compression to compression), in metres.</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Frequency f — cycles per second</dt><dd>In <strong>hertz</strong> (Hz). Set by the <em>source</em> — it does not change when the wave enters a new medium.</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Period T — seconds per cycle</dt><dd>T = 1/f. One crest passes every T seconds.</dd></div>
      </dl>

      <div class="formula">
        <span class="eq" data-display data-tex="v = f\lambda">v = f · λ</span>
        <span class="where">wave speed in m/s — each second, f wavelengths of length λ go past</span>
      </div>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        The wave speed v is a property of the <strong>medium</strong>: sound flies through steel
        (~5100 m/s) fifteen times faster than through air (343 m/s); waves on a tighter string run
        faster. Since f is fixed by the source, entering a new medium forces <strong>λ to
        adapt</strong>: λ = v/f.
      </p>

      <div class="callout callout-key">
        <div class="callout-title">Worked example</div>
        <p>Ocean swell arrives with crests every 8 s, spaced 12 m apart. How fast is it moving?</p>
        <p class="mono small">f = 1/T = 0.125 Hz · v = fλ = 0.125 × 12 = <b>1.5 m/s</b> — a slow walking pace, which is why swells feel so unhurried.</p>
      </div>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="types">4.2 · Transverse vs longitudinal</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Waves either wiggle side-to-side across their travel (transverse, like a rope) or squeeze-and-stretch along it (longitudinal, like sound).</p>
      <div class="table-scroll">
        <table class="data">
          <thead><tr><th></th><th>Transverse</th><th>Longitudinal</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td class="txt">Medium moves</td><td class="txt">⊥ to the travel direction</td><td class="txt">∥ to the travel direction</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Pattern</td><td class="txt">crests and troughs</td><td class="txt">compressions and rarefactions</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Examples</td><td class="txt">rope waves, light, water surface ripples</td><td class="txt">sound in air, slinky pushed end-to-end, P-waves in earthquakes</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="txt">Can polarise?</td><td class="txt">yes — polarisation is a transverse-only trick</td><td class="txt">no</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>

      <details class="dig dig-trap" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Common misconceptions</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p data-detail="tech">1. “The medium travels with the wave.” It does not — a floating duck bobs in place while the swell passes. Only the <em>disturbance</em> (and its energy) moves. Turn on “medium particles” in the simulator and watch a single dot: up and down, never along.</p>
        <p>2. “Higher frequency means faster wave.” Only if the medium lets it. In air, a 100 Hz bass note and a 10 kHz whistle travel at the same 343 m/s — the whistle just has a 100× shorter wavelength.</p>
        <p>3. “Sound is transverse because you can draw it as a wiggly line.” Oscilloscope traces plot pressure against time — they are <em>graphs</em>, not pictures of the air. In the air itself, sound is compressions marching along the direction of travel.</p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-wave-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">4.3 · Simulation — the wave bench</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Move the sliders and the wave responds instantly, including its speed, which is always frequency × wavelength.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Set amplitude, frequency and wavelength and watch v = fλ recompute live. Switch between
        the transverse drawing and the longitudinal one — same maths, different motion. Freeze the
        wave with <em>Pause</em> to measure a wavelength against the λ marker, and keep
        <em>medium particles</em> on to see that the dots only oscillate.
      </p>
    </section>

    <section class="section-tight wrap wrap-sim">
      <div class="panel reveal">
        <div class="panel-head">
          <h3 class="panel-title"><span class="dot" style="background:#d5b8d8"></span> Wave simulator</h3>
          <p class="panel-sub">y = A·sin(kx − ωt) · v = fλ</p>
          <div class="panel-actions">
            <div class="seg" id="wave-type" role="group" aria-label="Wave type">
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="transverse" aria-pressed="true">Transverse</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="longitudinal" aria-pressed="false">Longitudinal</button>
            </div>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" id="wave-pause" aria-pressed="false">Pause</button>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sim-grid">
          <div>
            <canvas id="sim-wave" class="sim-canvas" role="img"
                    aria-label="An animated travelling wave, drawn transverse or longitudinal, with wavelength and amplitude markers"></canvas>
            <div class="legend">
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a8d3e0"></i> the wave</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f6d36b"></i> medium particles</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#b5d777"></i> λ marker</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f8aebe"></i> A marker</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <div class="panel-body">
            <div class="ctl-stack">
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">A</span> amplitude</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="wave-Av">8 cm</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="wave-A" min="2" max="20" step="1" value="8" aria-label="Amplitude in centimetres">
              </div>
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">f</span> frequency</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="wave-fv">1.00 Hz</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="wave-f" min="0.2" max="3" step="0.1" value="1" aria-label="Frequency in hertz">
              </div>
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">λ</span> wavelength</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="wave-lamv">2.00 m</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="wave-lam" min="0.5" max="4" step="0.1" value="2" aria-label="Wavelength in metres">
              </div>
              <label class="ctl" style="grid-template-columns:auto 1fr;cursor:pointer">
                <input type="checkbox" id="wave-particles" checked style="accent-color:#f6d36b">
                <span class="ctl-label" style="font-size:.86rem">Show medium particles (they oscillate — they never travel)</span>
              </label>
            </div>

            <div class="readouts mt-4">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Wave speed v = fλ</span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="wave-v">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Period T = 1/f</span><span class="stat-value hl-amber" id="wave-T">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">ω = 2πf</span><span class="stat-value" id="wave-omega">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3 mono" data-detail="tech" id="wave-sub" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sound">4.4 · Sound</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Sound is a squeezing-and-stretching wave in air. Higher frequency means higher pitch; bigger amplitude means louder.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        Sound is a <strong>longitudinal mechanical wave</strong>: a loudspeaker cone punches
        compressions into the air, and your eardrum reads them back. It needs a medium — ring a
        bell under a vacuum jar and the hammer keeps moving in silence.
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Pitch is frequency.</strong> Human hearing spans about <strong>20 Hz – 20 kHz</strong>; below that is infrasound (elephants), above it ultrasound (bats, medical imaging). Concert pitch A4 = 440 Hz; every octave doubles f.</li>
        <li><strong>Loudness is amplitude</strong> (physically, intensity ∝ A²), measured on the logarithmic decibel scale: +10 dB ≈ twice as loud to the ear.</li>
        <li><strong>Speed belongs to the medium:</strong> 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, 1480 m/s in water, ~5100 m/s in steel. Warm air carries sound slightly faster — v ≈ 331 + 0.6·T(°C).</li>
      </ul>

      <div class="callout callout-key">
        <div class="callout-title">Worked examples</div>
        <p><strong>Wavelength of concert A.</strong> λ = v/f = 343/440 = <b>0.78 m</b> — about the width of a doorway, which is why bass (λ ≈ 3 m at 110 Hz) leaks through walls and treble does not.</p>
        <p><strong>How far is that storm?</strong> Flash, then thunder 6 s later: d = v·t = 343 × 6 ≈ <b>2 km</b>. (The rule of thumb: 3 s ≈ 1 km.)</p>
      </div>

      <details class="dig dig-real" data-detail="tech">
        <summary>Real world — the Doppler effect</summary>
        <div class="dig-body">
        <p>
          When a source moves, it chases its own wavefronts: in front, crests are squeezed
          together (higher f, higher pitch); behind, they are stretched (lower pitch). That is the
          <em>nee-oww</em> of a passing ambulance. The same shift, in light, is how we know the
          universe is expanding — distant galaxies are redshifted, their light waves stretched by
          recession.
        </p>
        </div>
      </details>

      <h2 class="h-sec" id="sim-sound-panel" style="scroll-margin-top:5rem">4.5 · Simulation — the tone player</h2>
      <p class="small muted" data-detail="plain" style="margin:.35rem 0 0">Press Play and hear exactly the note you see on the screen. Sweep the frequency upward and the pitch climbs with it.</p>
      <p data-detail="tech">
        This one you can <strong>hear</strong>. Sweep the frequency slider and watch the pitch name
        track across the note ruler — then press Play and listen to exactly the tone you see on the
        scope. Try the wave shapes: same pitch, different timbre (that is what makes a violin and
        a flute distinguishable at the same note). Headphones recommended; the sound is generated
        live in your browser, no audio files involved.
      </p>
    </section>

    <section class="section-tight wrap wrap-sim">
      <div class="panel reveal">
        <div class="panel-head">
          <h3 class="panel-title"><span class="dot" style="background:#d5b8d8"></span> Tone player — frequency vs pitch</h3>
          <p class="panel-sub">λ = v/f · v<sub>sound</sub> = 343 m/s at 20 °C</p>
          <div class="panel-actions">
            <div class="seg" id="snd-wave" role="group" aria-label="Wave shape">
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="sine" aria-pressed="true">Sine</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="square" aria-pressed="false">Square</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="sawtooth" aria-pressed="false">Saw</button>
              <button class="seg-btn" type="button" data-value="triangle" aria-pressed="false">Triangle</button>
            </div>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-snd-preset="110">A2</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-snd-preset="261.6">C4</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-primary" type="button" data-snd-preset="440">A4 · 440</button>
            <button class="btn btn-sm" type="button" data-snd-preset="880">A5</button>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="sim-grid">
          <div>
            <canvas id="sim-sound" class="sim-canvas" role="img"
                    aria-label="Oscilloscope trace of the selected tone with a note ruler underneath showing the current pitch"></canvas>
            <div class="legend">
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a8d3e0"></i> waveform (drawn)</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#b5d777"></i> live scope while playing</span>
              <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f6d36b"></i> pitch needle</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <div class="panel-body">
            <div class="ctl-stack">
              <div class="ctl">
                <span class="ctl-label"><span class="sym">f</span> frequency</span>
                <span class="ctl-value" id="snd-fv">440 Hz</span>
                <input class="range ctl-range" type="range" id="snd-f" min="55" max="1760" step="1" value="440" aria-label="Tone frequency in hertz">
              </div>
              <button class="btn btn-primary" type="button" id="snd-play" aria-pressed="false">Play tone</button>
            </div>

            <div class="readouts mt-4">
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Pitch (nearest note)</span><span class="stat-value hl-cyan" id="snd-note">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">λ in air</span><span class="stat-value hl-amber" id="snd-lambda">—</span></div>
              <div class="stat"><span class="stat-label">Period</span><span class="stat-value" id="snd-period">—</span></div>
            </div>
            <p class="sim-note mt-3 mono" data-detail="tech" id="snd-sub" style="overflow-wrap:anywhere">—</p>
            <p class="sim-note mt-2" id="snd-status">—</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section wrap wrap-narrow prose">
      <h2 class="h-sec" id="check">4.6 · Check your understanding</h2>

      <details class="check">
        <summary>A wave has f = 10 Hz and λ = 0.5 m. Find v and T.</summary>
        <div class="answer">v = fλ = 10 × 0.5 = <b>5 m/s</b>; T = 1/f = <b>0.1 s</b>.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Sound enters water, where it travels about 4.3× faster than in air. What happens to f and λ?</summary>
        <div class="answer"><b>f is unchanged</b> (the source still vibrates at the same rate — crests cannot pile up at the boundary), so λ must grow 4.3×: λ = v/f. Faster medium, longer wavelength, same pitch.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>Which is longitudinal: (a) a guitar string’s wave, (b) the sound the string makes, (c) light from the stage lamps?</summary>
        <div class="answer">Only <b>(b)</b>. The string vibrates perpendicular to its length (transverse) and light is transverse too — but the pressure wave the string launches into the air is compressions along the direction of travel: longitudinal.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>You see lightning and hear the thunder 9 s later. How far away was the strike?</summary>
        <div class="answer">Light is essentially instantaneous; sound took 9 s: d = 343 × 9 ≈ <b>3.1 km</b>.</div>
      </details>
      <details class="check">
        <summary>On the tone player, doubling f from 220 to 440 Hz changes what you hear how? And what happens to λ in air?</summary>
        <div class="answer">The pitch rises exactly <b>one octave</b> (220 Hz is A3, 440 Hz is A4 — the same note name). Since v stays 343 m/s, λ <b>halves</b>: from 1.56 m to 0.78 m.</div>
      </details>

/* EMC Physics - self-hosted webfonts.
   ONE family for the whole site: G8321 by Coji Morishita (SIL OFL 1.1),
   three committed weights:
     100 Thin    - oversized display numerals (score grade, topic watermark, ring %)
     400 Regular - body copy, prose, labels (the site's default)
     700 Bold    - headings, buttons, nav, micro-labels
   Titles additionally lead with 'fot-yuruka-std': a PRIVATELY licensed face
   that only machines holding it locally can render (see vendor/fonts/README.md) -
   everywhere else titles cleanly fall back to G8321 Bold, the same family as
   the body. No other webfonts are used. */

@font-face {
  font-family: 'G8321';
  src: url('../vendor/fonts/g8321-100.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-weight: 100;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}

}
